warmup.q: The report service's log says "fetch took 46 ms" for a few slow requests. What can a JFR recording of the same minutes tell you that the log line can't?
options: Nothing more: the log line already has the duration
Whether a garbage-collection pause, a wait for a lock or a burst of allocation happened at the same moment, on the same clock
What the document store did inside its own program
Which line of the document store's code was slow
warmup.why: JFR records the JVM's own events, such as garbage-collection pauses, waits for locks, sampled allocations and sampled stacks, each with a timestamp and a thread, next to any events you add. So you can see what else happened while the slow call ran. It can't look inside another program: the document store would need a recording of its own.

opening:
Back in the restaurant, a long night is over. A customer says the soup took forty minutes, and the cook remembers making it in six. Both can be true: the bowl may have waited for the only waiter, or for the kitchen to finish washing up. To settle it, you'd want one log of everything the kitchen did, every order, wait and wash-up, on one clock. It must be cheap enough to keep every night, because nobody knows which night will go wrong.

The JVM, the program that runs your Java and Kotlin, keeps a log like that. It's already in your JDK, and it's called JDK Flight Recorder.

The easy trap is the tool we all reach for first: a timer and a log line around the slow call. It answers one question about one call, on a clock of its own. Lesson 4 made one hot spot cheaper once we knew where it was. Now we need to find where a running program spends its time. In this lesson, we'll record the report service, question the recording, add our own notes to it and watch events live. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.
closing:
We started with a soup that took forty minutes in the customer's story and six in the cook's. JFR keeps the log that settles it: the JVM's events and ours, on one clock, cheap enough to leave on all night, and dumped without stopping anything.

Now look in your own code for a log line that prints a duration, such as took {} ms. Each one could be an event with fields and a threshold, sitting on the same timeline as the GC.

Next, we'll take thousands of samples instead of forty. How does a sampling profiler find where the time goes, and why does it draw its answer as a flame graph?

sections.h: JFR records what the JVM did, on one clock, cheap enough to leave on
sections.html:
Start with the hand-made answer. The report service from the earlier lessons fetches each document from a document store, another program that keeps the documents and answers over the network. Some fetches are slow, so we wrap one in a timer and log fetch took 46 ms. That's one number for one call. It can't say whether every thread was paused for a garbage collection at that moment. (The garbage collector, or GC, is the part of the JVM that frees memory nobody uses.) Nor can it say whether the thread waited for a lock, a guard that lets one thread at a time into a piece of code, or whether something allocated a lot of memory that second.

JDK Flight Recorder (JFR) is a recorder built into HotSpot, the JVM in every OpenJDK build. It writes events: small records with a start time, often a duration, the thread, and usually a stack trace, the chain of method calls that led there. HotSpot has events for GC pauses, JIT compilations (the JVM turning busy methods into machine code, as lessons 1 and 2 showed), waits for locks, file and network reads, and samples of running threads and of allocation. Your code can add events of its own. All of them go into one timeline, on one clock. That's the kitchen's log for the whole night.

A recording is one session of that log, with its settings and limits. It keeps events in memory buffers and moves them to disk in chunks. Picture a log book that tears out its oldest pages when it's full: maxage says how far back to keep, maxsize how many bytes. Set neither, and the JVM keeps 250 MB. You can start a recording when the JVM starts, or on a JVM that's already running:

java -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=rec.jfr,settings=profile -jar app.jar

jcmd <pid> JFR.start name=reports settings=profile     # on a JVM that's already running
jcmd <pid> JFR.dump name=reports filename=reports.jfr  # copy what it has so far to a file
jcmd <pid> JFR.stop name=reports

jcmd is a tool in the JDK that sends commands to a running JVM, and <pid> is the process id, the number the operating system gives each running program. On JDK 25, the report service answered the first command like this:

Started recording 1. No limit specified, using maxsize=250MB as default.

Use jcmd 30725 JFR.dump name=reports filename=FILEPATH to copy recording data to file.

A dump copies the pages written so far and stops nothing. That's why a recording that's always on pays off: when something goes wrong, the last hour is already in the book.

settings picks a configuration file. default.jfc describes itself as "safe for continuous use in production environments, typically less than 1 % overhead". profile.jfc says "typically around 2 % overhead" and records more. In JDK 25, default samples running threads every 20 ms, takes up to 150 allocation samples a second and records lock waits of 20 ms or more. profile samples every 10 ms, takes 300 allocation samples a second and records lock waits from 10 ms.

The first question to ask any recording is what's in it. jfr summary, from the JDK's jfr tool, lists every event type with a count. For the Try it below, four threads, lines of work that run side by side inside the program, wrote reports for 4 seconds under profile. Part of the summary:

 Event Type                              Count  Size (bytes)
=============================================================
 jdk.GCPhaseParallel                      1951         50576
 workbench.StoreCall                      1361         35305
 jdk.ObjectAllocationSample               1207         16978
 jdk.ThreadSleep                           560         10078
 ...
 jdk.ExecutionSample                        40           400
 jdk.JavaMonitorEnter                       29           667

workbench.StoreCall is ours, one event per call to the document store, and section 3 builds it. Everything else is the JVM's, and only the garbage collector's paperwork outnumbers us. Notice how few execution samples there are. The threads spent most of the time asleep, waiting for the store, and the sampler only counts threads that are running Java code. Keep that 40 in mind for the end of the lesson.

A cheap recording that's always on is evidence you already have. Dump it instead of restarting.

The summary says what the log holds. Next, we'll ask it a question.

try.title: Record the busy report service
steps: Read JfrDemo and skim ReportWorkload next to it. Four threads each count the words in 2,000 short lines, ask a fake document store for a document (it sleeps a few milliseconds, longer for shelf-7), and on every tenth document hold a shared archive lock for 15 ms.
Predict which event type will have the highest count, and roughly how many execution samples 4 seconds will give.
Run it from labs/. The demo starts a second JVM with -XX:StartFlightRecording and prints the path of the .jfr file.
Run jfr summary on that file (the demo prints the command).

code.title: JfrDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.performance.l05; import java.nio.file.Path; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; /** * Runs ReportWorkload for 4 seconds in a second JVM started with * -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=build/perf05.jfr,settings=profile * and tells you where the recording is. */ public class JfrDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { if (args.length > 0 && args[0].equals("child")) { ReportWorkload.run(4); return; } Path file = Path.of("build", "perf05.jfr").toAbsolutePath(); String java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java"); List<String> cmd = new ArrayList<>(List.of(java, "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=" + file + ",settings=profile", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), JfrDemo.class.getName(), "child")); Process p = new ProcessBuilder(cmd).inheritIO().start(); p.waitFor(); System.out.println("recording written to " + file); System.out.println("try: jfr summary " + file); } }

alt.title: JfrDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l05 import jdk.jfr.Category import jdk.jfr.Description import jdk.jfr.Event import jdk.jfr.Label import jdk.jfr.Name import java.nio.file.Path import java.util.concurrent.ThreadLocalRandom import kotlin.concurrent.thread // Kotlin twin of JfrDemo.java (with its workload and event in this one file). It runs the workload // for 4 seconds in a second JVM started with -XX:StartFlightRecording and writes build/perf05-kt.jfr. @Name("workbench.StoreCall") @Label("Store Call") @Category("Workbench", "Reports") @Description("A call to the document store while writing a report") class KStoreCallEvent : Event() { @Label("Shelf") var shelf: String? = null // a Kotlin property: JFR records its field @Label("Words") var words = 0L @Label("Found") var found = false } private val archive = Any() fun kCountWords(line: String): Long = line.split(' ').size.toLong() // allocates: a new String for every word fun kCallStore(shelf: String, doc: Int): Long { val event = KStoreCallEvent() event.begin() Thread.sleep(ThreadLocalRandom.current().nextInt(2, if (shelf == "shelf-7") 40 else 12).toLong()) val found = doc % 17 != 0 val words = if (found) 200L + doc % 3_000 else 0L event.end() if (event.shouldCommit()) { // skip the field work when no recording wants it event.shelf = shelf event.words = words event.found = found event.commit() } return words } fun kRunWorkload(seconds: Int) { val until = System.nanoTime() + seconds * 1_000_000_000L val workers = (0 until 4).map { w -> thread(name = "report-$w") { var sink = 0L var i = 0 while (System.nanoTime() < until) { for (k in 0 until 2_000) sink += kCountWords("page ${(k + i) % 9_000} of the weekly report on rain") sink += kCallStore("shelf-${i % 10}", i) if (i % 10 == w) synchronized(archive) { Thread.sleep(15) } // writing to the shared archive i++ } if (sink == 42L) println() } } workers.forEach { it.join() } } fun main(args: Array<String>) { if (args.firstOrNull() == "child") return kRunWorkload(4) val file = Path.of("build", "perf05-kt.jfr").toAbsolutePath() val java = ProcessHandle.current().info().command().orElse("java") ProcessBuilder(java, "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=$file,settings=profile", "-cp", System.getProperty("java.class.path"), "workbench.performance.l05.JfrDemoKt", "child") .inheritIO().start().waitFor() println("recording written to $file") println("try: jfr summary $file") }

try.expect: The JVM prints its "Started recording" lines, then the demo prints the file path; the file was about 440 KB here. In the run above, jfr summary counted 1,951 jdk.GCPhaseParallel, 1,361 workbench.StoreCall, 1,207 jdk.ObjectAllocationSample and 560 jdk.ThreadSleep events, but only 40 jdk.ExecutionSample, because the threads spend most of their time asleep. Your counts will differ from run to run.

sections.h: Asking the recording questions with jfr view and jfr print
sections.html:
Three subcommands of the jfr tool cover most days. You've met jfr summary. jfr view <view> <file> prints a ready-made report: views arrived in JDK 21, and jfr help view lists the dozens there are now. jfr print prints events one by one.

Three views answer the questions from the opening. Did threads wait for each other? contention-by-site groups the waits to enter a synchronized block, the lock Java takes with the synchronized keyword, by where they happened:

                                 Contention by Site

StackTrace                                                     Count    Avg.    Max.
-------------------------------------------------------------- ----- ------- -------
workbench.performance.l05.ReportWorkload.reportLoop(int, long)    28 15.5 ms 34.0 ms
jdk.jfr.internal.PlatformRecorder.periodicTask()                   1 11.0 ms 11.0 ms

Twenty-eight waits at the shared archive lock, 15.5 ms on average: about the 15 ms each writer holds it. The second line is JFR's own housekeeping thread, which once got stuck behind a lock of its own.

Who allocates? allocation-by-site adds up the allocation samples by the method that did the allocating:

Method                                                               Allocation Pressure
-------------------------------------------------------------------- -------------------
java.util.Arrays.copyOfRange(byte[], int, int)                                    36.56%
java.lang.StringLatin1.newString(byte[], int, int)                                33.31%
jdk.internal.misc.Unsafe.allocateUninitializedArray(Class, int)                    9.76%
java.util.ArrayList.grow(int)                                                      9.51%
java.lang.String.split(char, int, boolean)                                         6.27%

Every line is JDK code, and every one is the inside of String.split, which our countWords calls 2,000 times per document. A view names the method that allocated, not the line of yours that asked for it. Lesson 7 walks down the stack traces to find that line.

Did the JVM stop every thread? gc-pauses gives the count, the total and the longest pause. And lesson 2 promised a view for the JIT's lost bets, deoptimizations-by-reason:

Reason                                                                     Count
------------------------------------------------------ -------------------------
unstable_if                                                                    7
bimorphic_or_optimized_type_check                                              4
class_check                                                                    4
intrinsic_or_type_checked_inlining                                             1

Sixteen in a program that ran 4 seconds is the burst at start-up that lesson 2 described. A steady stream hours after start is the thing to worry about.

Each view is a query over events, and jfr view --verbose shows the query. Pass the name of an event type as the view, such as jfr view workbench.StoreCall rec.jfr, and you get a table of those events. On a running JVM, jcmd <pid> JFR.view hot-methods prints a view without writing a file. jfr print --events workbench.StoreCall --stack-depth 2 rec.jfr prints events one at a time with every field; add --json for a script.

JDK Mission Control (JMC) is the desktop app for the same files: timelines, flame graphs of the samples (lesson 6 explains those) and an automatic analysis. It's developed in the openjdk/jmc project and downloaded separately, from builds that several vendors publish. The jfr tool is enough for everything in this lesson, and it's already in your JDK.

Read jfr summary first, then ask one question per view.

Before you send a recording to anyone, look at what else it holds. The demo's file has 169 jdk.InitialEnvironmentVariable events and the full command line. A recording remembers more than you told it, and environment variables are where programs often keep passwords. JDK 27 adds redaction inside the JVM (JEP 536, -XX:FlightRecorderOptions:redact-argument=...). On older JDKs, check the file first, or share the views instead of the file.

The figure shows where all these events go. So far they've been the JVM's, apart from one type we haven't explained yet.

steps: Using the file from the last Try it: where do threads wait for locks, and for how long at most? Run jfr view contention-by-site <file>.
Which methods allocate the most? Run jfr view allocation-by-site <file>. Which line of ReportWorkload calls all of them?
Which shelf has slow store calls? Run jfr view workbench.StoreCall <file> and look at the Duration column, then jfr print --events workbench.StoreCall --stack-depth 2 <file> | head -20.

In the table, shelf-7 calls take up to about 40 ms; on a busy machine some other shelves stretch past their 12 ms too. jfr print shows each event's fields and the two frames that called it, with line numbers.

sections.h: Your own events add the service's notes to the same log
sections.html:
An event of your own is a class that extends jdk.jfr.Event. Its fields are the data, and annotations give it a stable name and labels for the tools. Here's the demo's event for one call to the document store. The demo's store is fake and only sleeps, so the code around the call is shown the way a real service would write it:

Java
@Name("workbench.StoreCall")
@Label("Store Call")
@Category({"Workbench", "Reports"})
public class StoreCallEvent extends Event {
    @Label("Shelf") String shelf;
    @Label("Words") long words;
    @Label("Found") boolean found;
}

StoreCallEvent event = new StoreCallEvent();
event.begin();                                  // 1. start the clock
String text = store.fetch(shelf, title);
event.end();                                    // 2. stop it
if (event.shouldCommit()) {                     // 3. false if no recording wants it
    event.shelf = shelf;
    event.words = text == null ? 0 : countWords(text);
    event.found = text != null;
    event.commit();                             // 4. write it, with a stack trace
}
Kotlin
@Name("workbench.StoreCall")
@Label("Store Call")
@Category("Workbench", "Reports")
class KStoreCallEvent : Event() {
    @Label("Shelf") var shelf: String? = null
    @Label("Words") var words = 0L
    @Label("Found") var found = false
}

val event = KStoreCallEvent()
event.begin()                                   // 1. start the clock
val text = store.fetch(shelf, title)
event.end()                                     // 2. stop it
if (event.shouldCommit()) {                     // 3. false if no recording wants it
    event.shelf = shelf
    event.words = if (text == null) 0 else countWords(text)
    event.found = text != null
    event.commit()                              // 4. write it, with a stack trace
}

Read it from the top. @Name is the name that recordings and tools use to find the event. @Label and @Category are what JMC and jfr view display. begin() starts the event's clock and end() stops it, so its duration covers the store call. shouldCommit() returns true only if some recording has this event switched on and the duration passes that recording's threshold, the shortest duration it keeps. Only then do we fill in the fields and commit(), which writes the event with the thread and a stack trace taken at that moment.

The shouldCommit() check matters because Java works out each field's value before the assignment, and countWords isn't free. When no recording wants the event, the check skips that work, and the event costs almost nothing. In the kitchen, it's a note the cook writes only when somebody is keeping the log.

Kotlin needs nothing special. JFR records the field behind each Kotlin property, and a Java annotation such as @Label on a property lands on that field.

Compare it with the log line from section 1. The event has fields you can filter, instead of text you have to parse. A recording can also keep only the slow ones: +workbench.StoreCall#threshold=30ms on the command line keeps calls of 30 ms or more. The + is needed because your event isn't listed in the .jfc file. Leave it out, and JDK 25 warns The .jfc option/setting 'workbench.StoreCall#threshold' doesn't exist. and ignores it. Above all, the event sits on the same timeline as the GC pauses and lock waits, with the same thread names. jfr view workbench.StoreCall showed the demo's events like this (trimmed to two rows):

Start Time Duration Event Thread Stack Trace                                                     Shelf   Words Found
---------- -------- ------------ --------------------------------------------------------------- ------- ----- -----
07:47:36    18.3 ms report-2     workbench.performance.l05.ReportWorkload.callStore(String, int) shelf-1   201  true
07:47:36    46.6 ms report-3     workbench.performance.l05.ReportWorkload.callStore(String, int) shelf-7   207  true

Reading events back in code is short. RecordingFile.readAllEvents(path) returns every event in a file. Each RecordedEvent has getEventType().getName(), getDuration(), getString("shelf"), getBoolean("found") and friends. That's the lab.

Fill an event's fields inside shouldCommit(). When nobody records, the event costs almost nothing.

Check yourself: your event sits in a method that runs 50,000 times a second, and no recording has it switched on. What does shouldCommit() return, and what does it save you? (It returns false, and it saves you the work of computing the fields. commit() would have written nothing anyway.)

A recording answers questions after the fact. Sometimes you want the answers while the program is still running.

try.title: Keep only the slow calls
steps: In JfrDemo.java, change the recording option to "-XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=" + file + ",settings=profile,+workbench.StoreCall#threshold=30ms" (note the +).
Predict: out of about 1,300 store calls, roughly how many will be recorded now, and from which shelves?
Run the demo again, then jfr summary and jfr view workbench.StoreCall on the new file.
try.expect: Only a few dozen workbench.StoreCall events remain, all 30 ms or longer: 50 in one run here, 33 of them from shelf-7, whose fake store sleeps up to 40 ms. The other 17 came from shelves that sleep at most 12 ms; the busy machine stretched those sleeps past 30 ms, which is a finding of its own. The JVM's own events are unchanged, because the threshold is a setting of the recording, not of your code.

sections.h: Watching events live, and what JDK 25 added
sections.html:
jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingStream, in the JDK since version 14, hands the same events to your own code while the JVM runs:

Java
try (RecordingStream rs = new RecordingStream()) {
    rs.enable("workbench.StoreCall").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(35));   // only the slow ones
    rs.enable("jdk.GarbageCollection");
    rs.onEvent("workbench.StoreCall", e -> System.out.printf("slow store call: %s, %d ms%n",
            e.getString("shelf"), e.getDuration().toMillis()));
    rs.onEvent("jdk.GarbageCollection", e -> System.out.printf("GC: %s, %.1f ms pause total%n",
            e.getString("name"), e.getDuration("sumOfPauses").toNanos() / 1e6));
    rs.startAsync();                     // events arrive on a background thread
    ReportWorkload.run(3);
}
Kotlin
RecordingStream().use { rs ->
    rs.enable("workbench.StoreCall").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(35))   // only the slow ones
    rs.enable("jdk.GarbageCollection")
    rs.onEvent("workbench.StoreCall") { e ->
        println("slow store call: ${e.getString("shelf")}, ${e.duration.toMillis()} ms")
    }
    rs.onEvent("jdk.GarbageCollection") { e ->
        println("GC: %s, %.1f ms pause total".format(e.getString("name"), e.getDuration("sumOfPauses").toNanos() / 1e6))
    }
    rs.startAsync()                      // events arrive on a background thread
    kRunWorkload(3)
}

Events reach the callbacks in batches, about once a second, on a background thread. That suits turning JVM events into numbers for a dashboard, such as GC pause time per minute. It's not a hook into the busy path of your code. One run of StreamingDemo printed lines like these:

slow store call: shelf-1, 46 ms
GC: G1New, 16.3 ms pause total
slow store call: shelf-7, 155 ms
slow store call: shelf-9, 130 ms

Shelf 7 is slow on purpose. The others were slow because the machine was: more than 30 other busy programs shared its four cores that day, so a 12 ms sleep often lasted much longer. A stream can't tell which slowness you meant. That's one more reason to have the CPU and GC events on the same clock as your own.

JDK 25 added three profiling features to JFR, and all of these ran here on JDK 25.

  • Method timing and tracing (JEP 520) counts and times chosen methods with no change to the code. -XX:StartFlightRecording:method-timing=workbench.performance.l05.ReportWorkload::countWords,report-on-exit=method-timing printed a table as the JVM exited: 2,024,000 calls of countWords, 0.001160 ms on average, 88.6 ms at most. That maximum is a call that waited out a GC pause or a busy CPU; the average is the cost of the call. The filter can also name a whole class or an annotation.
  • CPU-time sampling (JEP 509), experimental and only on Linux, samples each thread by the CPU time it uses. Switch on jdk.CPUTimeSample (for example jdk.CPUTimeSample#enabled=true,jdk.CPUTimeSample#throttle=10ms) and read it with jfr view cpu-time-hot-methods. On the report workload it took 64 samples in 4 seconds, a quarter of them in String.split.
  • Cooperative sampling (JEP 518) changes how the JVM takes execution samples inside. There's nothing to configure.

report-on-exit=<view> prints any view when the JVM exits, so a test run can leave a report in its log. JDK 21 doesn't know the option and says so.

Here's where today's tool stops. JFR's classic sampler took 40 execution samples in 4 seconds of a busy program. That's enough to spot a method that takes most of the time, and far too few to see what that method does inside. Lesson 6 brings in a profiler that takes thousands.

code.html: package workbench.performance.l05; import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingStream; import java.time.Duration; /** Watches the running JVM with JFR event streaming: slow store calls and garbage collections, live. */ public class StreamingDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { try (RecordingStream rs = new RecordingStream()) { rs.enable("workbench.StoreCall").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(35)); // only the slow ones rs.enable("jdk.GarbageCollection"); rs.onEvent("workbench.StoreCall", e -> System.out.printf("slow store call: %s, %d ms%n", e.getString("shelf"), e.getDuration().toMillis())); rs.onEvent("jdk.GarbageCollection", e -> System.out.printf("GC: %s, %.1f ms pause total%n", e.getString("name"), e.getDuration("sumOfPauses").toNanos() / 1e6)); rs.startAsync(); // events arrive on a background thread ReportWorkload.run(3); Thread.sleep(1_500); // let the last flush reach us } } }

alt.title: StreamingDemo.kt
alt.html: package workbench.performance.l05 import jdk.jfr.consumer.RecordingStream import java.time.Duration // Kotlin twin of StreamingDemo.java: slow store calls and garbage collections, live, from inside the JVM. fun main() { RecordingStream().use { rs -> rs.enable("workbench.StoreCall").withThreshold(Duration.ofMillis(35)) // only the slow ones rs.enable("jdk.GarbageCollection") rs.onEvent("workbench.StoreCall") { e -> println("slow store call: ${e.getString("shelf")}, ${e.duration.toMillis()} ms") } rs.onEvent("jdk.GarbageCollection") { e -> println("GC: %s, %.1f ms pause total".format(e.getString("name"), e.getDuration("sumOfPauses").toNanos() / 1e6)) } rs.startAsync() // events arrive on a background thread kRunWorkload(3) Thread.sleep(1_500) // let the last flush reach us } }

try.expect: Lines such as slow store call: shelf-7, 39 ms arrive in batches, mixed with lines such as GC: G1New, 16.3 ms pause total. shelf-7 shows up most, between 35 and 50 ms; other shelves appear when the machine is busy. For the JDK 25 step, run java '-XX:StartFlightRecording:method-timing=workbench.performance.l05.ReportWorkload::countWords,report-on-exit=method-timing' -cp performance/build/classes/java/demo workbench.performance.l05.JfrDemo child from labs/ after the Gradle run has compiled the demos. It ends with a Method Timing table for countWords: about two million calls, around a microsecond each.

compare.title: A custom JFR event in Java and Kotlin

java.title: StoreCallEvent.java
java.html: @Name("workbench.StoreCall") @Label("Store Call") @Category({"Workbench", "Reports"}) public class StoreCallEvent extends Event { @Label("Shelf") String shelf; @Label("Words") long words; @Label("Found") boolean found; } StoreCallEvent event = new StoreCallEvent(); event.begin(); // 1. start the clock String text = store.fetch(shelf, title); event.end(); // 2. stop it if (event.shouldCommit()) { // 3. false if no recording wants it event.shelf = shelf; event.words = text == null ? 0 : countWords(text); event.found = text != null; event.commit(); // 4. write it, with a stack trace }

kotlin.title: JfrDemo.kt
kotlin.html: @Name("workbench.StoreCall") @Label("Store Call") @Category("Workbench", "Reports") class KStoreCallEvent : Event() { @Label("Shelf") var shelf: String? = null @Label("Words") var words = 0L @Label("Found") var found = false } val event = KStoreCallEvent() event.begin() // 1. start the clock val text = store.fetch(shelf, title) event.end() // 2. stop it if (event.shouldCommit()) { // 3. false if no recording wants it event.shelf = shelf event.words = if (text == null) 0 else countWords(text) event.found = text != null event.commit() // 4. write it, with a stack trace }

compare.note: The same event, recorded the same way. A Kotlin var compiles to a private field plus a getter and a setter, and JFR records the field. A Java annotation such as @Label placed on a Kotlin property goes to that field, because FIELD is the only one of its targets a property can use. @Category takes an array, written {"Workbench", "Reports"} in Java and as plain arguments in Kotlin. Both versions produce the same event type, workbench.StoreCall, so the same jfr view works on either recording. The Kotlin field for the shelf is a nullable String?, because an event is created empty and filled in later.

worked.title: Explain a slow evening with one dump

steps.say: The report service's slowest requests got slower at 14:02, and it runs a continuous recording. Check which recordings exist, then dump the last 10 minutes without restarting anything.
steps.code: jcmd 4711 JFR.check jcmd 4711 JFR.dump name=1 maxage=10m filename=/tmp/reports-1402.jfr

steps.say: First question: did the JVM stop every thread? gc-pauses answers in one screen. If the longest pause is a few milliseconds, the GC isn't your 200 ms.

Second question: did threads wait for each other? contention-by-site lists the synchronized blocks that threads waited to enter, with counts and the longest wait. A 180 ms maximum on the archive lock would explain a lot.

Third question: which calls were slow, and on which shelf? Your own event answers, on the same clock. Self-check: if a slow store call and a long lock wait share a thread name and a timestamp, which one do you look at first? (The lock wait: it happens inside your own process, and the store call may only look slow because its thread was waiting.)
steps.code: jfr print --events workbench.StoreCall /tmp/reports-1402.jfr | grep -B3 -A6 'duration = [0-9][0-9][0-9] ms'

steps.say: Write the finding down with the evidence, and attach the views, not the file: the file holds environment variables and the command line.

lab.title: Record your own event and read it back
steps: Open DocumentStore, the given interface for the program that keeps the documents, and Librarian, the report service's class that asks it for a document by shelf and title. Run the tests. Five of the six fail. Each one starts a real JFR recording, makes six lookups, writes a real .jfr file and reads it back. The one that passes checks that lookup still returns the store's answer.
Make LookupEvent an event named workbench.Lookup, with a label, a category that includes Reports, and three labelled fields: shelf, title and found.
In Librarian.lookup, record one event per call. Its duration must cover the store call: the test's basement shelf takes 100 ms to answer, and a test checks for it.
Write LookupReport.missingByShelf and LookupReport.slowestShelf with RecordingFile. The file also holds jdk.ThreadSleep events, so filter by event name.
Run the tests until all six pass.
hints: The annotations are @Name, @Label, @Category and @Description from jdk.jfr. The fields can stay package-private.
Call begin() right before store.fetch(...) and end() right after it. Fill the fields and commit() inside if (event.shouldCommit()). found is text != null.
RecordingFile.readAllEvents(path) returns a List<RecordedEvent>. Filter on e.getEventType().getName(), then use e.getBoolean("found"), e.getString("shelf") and e.getDuration().
Map.merge(shelf, 1L, Long::sum) counts per key in one line. A TreeMap keeps the result sorted, which makes failures easier to read.

drill.title: From memory: event, recording, query
drill.prompt: Close this page. Write (1) an event class ReportWriteEvent named workbench.ReportWrite with a title field, (2) the code that times writing one report with it, and (3) the two shell commands that start a recording on JVM 4711 and later write it to reports.jfr. Then check against the answer.

answer.html: @Name("workbench.ReportWrite") @Label("Report Write") @Category({"Workbench", "Reports"}) class ReportWriteEvent extends Event { @Label("Title") String title; } ReportWriteEvent event = new ReportWriteEvent(); event.begin(); writer.write(report); event.end(); if (event.shouldCommit()) { event.title = report.title(); event.commit(); } // jcmd 4711 JFR.start name=reports settings=profile // jcmd 4711 JFR.dump name=reports filename=reports.jfr

alt.html: @Name("workbench.ReportWrite") @Label("Report Write") @Category("Workbench", "Reports") class ReportWriteEvent : Event() { @Label("Title") var title: String? = null } val event = ReportWriteEvent() event.begin() writer.write(report) event.end() if (event.shouldCommit()) { event.title = report.title event.commit() } // jcmd 4711 JFR.start name=reports settings=profile // jcmd 4711 JFR.dump name=reports filename=reports.jfr

recap: JFR is built into HotSpot and records timestamped events (GC, JIT, locks, CPU and allocation samples, I/O) on one timeline. Start it with -XX:StartFlightRecording or jcmd <pid> JFR.start, and copy data out with JFR.dump, which stops nothing.

default.jfc is meant to stay on (under 1% overhead, by its own description); profile.jfc samples twice as often and keeps shorter lock waits, so use it for short investigations. Set maxage or maxsize, or the JVM keeps 250 MB.
jfr summary shows what a file holds, jfr view (JDK 21+) prints reports such as contention-by-site, allocation-by-site, gc-pauses and deoptimizations-by-reason, and jfr print shows single events.
Your own events extend jdk.jfr.Event: begin, end, shouldCommit, commit. They share the timeline with the JVM's events. RecordingFile reads them back; RecordingStream delivers them live.
JDK 25 adds method timing (JEP 520), experimental CPU-time sampling on Linux (JEP 509) and report-on-exit. Recordings hold environment variables and the command line; JDK 27 can redact them.

The limit: JFR's classic sampler took 40 stack samples in 4 seconds here, and its views name the JDK method rather than your line. Seeing where the time goes inside a method takes a profiler with many more samples (lesson 6).

explain.prompt: A teammate asks why you'd add a JFR event around the call to the document store when there's already a log line with the duration. Explain the difference in your own words.
explain.answer: The log line is one number per call, written as text, and it's always on. A JFR event has fields, so I can filter and group by shelf or outcome without parsing anything. It costs almost nothing when no recording wants it, because I fill the fields only after shouldCommit(), and a recording can keep only the slow ones with a threshold. Most of all, it lands on the same timeline as the JVM's own events. So for a slow call I can see whether a GC pause, a lock wait or a burst of allocation happened on the same thread at the same moment. A log line can't tell me that.

deeper.html:
JFR's views are queries, kept in the JDK source in a file called view.ini. For example, hot-methods counts ExecutionSample events grouped by their top frame, and deoptimizations-by-reason counts Deoptimization events grouped by reason. jfr view --verbose prints the query a view runs, which helps when you build your own analysis with RecordingFile.

The demo got only 40 execution samples in 4 seconds. Its threads sleep most of the time, and the classic sampler records threads that are running Java code, not sleeping ones. On a machine shared with many busy programs, a running thread may also be waiting for a CPU core when the sampler looks. That's one reason lesson 6 brings in async-profiler, which samples with signals and timers, and why JDK 25 added the CPU-time sampler.

jfr has more subcommands: jfr configure builds a custom .jfc file from options, jfr scrub writes a copy of a recording without chosen events, jfr assemble and jfr disassemble join and split chunk files, and jfr metadata lists every event type and field.

To record a whole test run, add -XX:StartFlightRecording:filename=build/test.jfr to the test JVM's arguments. On JDK 25, adding report-on-exit=allocation-by-site prints the allocation report straight into the build log, so a reviewer can see it without opening any file.
